title: Five Signs Your Workforce Strategy May Be Falling Behind Your Business Strategy
summary: A strong business strategy requires a strong workforce strategy. Discover five signs your workforce approach may need attention.
body_markdown:
Business strategies evolve constantly. Organizations enter new markets, launch new services, and pursue growth opportunities. And yet, workforce strategies don’t always evolve at the same pace.


This can create a growing disconnect between where the business wants to go and whether the workforce is equipped to get it there. If any of the following challenges sound familiar, it may be time to take[a closer look at workforce readiness.](https://www.cbiz.com/insights/article/why-more-employers-are-reassessing-workforce-readiness-in-2027)


## Critical Roles Are Staying Open Longer


When vacancies remain open longer than anticipated, the impact often extends beyond recruiting. Projects may slow, existing employees may take on additional responsibilities, and managers may spend valuable time filling operational gaps instead of focusing on strategic objectives.


For organizations without a dedicated recruiting function, workforce growth plans may also depend on having the right recruiting support.[CBIZ Recruitment Process Outsourcing](https://talentsolutions.cbiz.com/employer-services/recruitment-process-outsourcing) can help strengthen recruiting capacity while bolstering workforce growth objectives.


## Growth Plans Depend on Future Hiring Success


Many organizations build business plans around anticipated workforce growth. The approach makes sense in theory, but the risk emerges when growth projections rely heavily on hiring that has not yet occurred.


If future revenue targets, expansion plans, or operational improvements depend on filling multiple critical positions, workforce readiness can become a key business risk. Organizations should routinely evaluate whether workforce growth is keeping pace with strategic growth.


## Employees Are Carrying More Than They Should


When workforce capacity falls behind business demand, employees often absorb the difference. At first, the effects may seem manageable. Over time, however, these temporary solutions can become permanent operating models.


Increased workloads can contribute to burnout, lower productivity, and reduced employee satisfaction.[Recent workforce research highlighted by CBIZ](https://www.cbiz.com/insights/article/navigating-the-2026-workforce-landscape-five-key-trends-for-success) found that 48% of workers identify overwhelming workloads as a primary workplace concern. They may also indicate that current staffing levels are no longer aligned with organizational demands.


## Retention Challenges Are Emerging in Key Roles


Not all turnover carries the same level of risk. Losing employees in business-critical positions can create significant operational disruption. Organizations that consistently struggle to retain employees in critical roles should view the issue as a strategic concern rather than an isolated workforce challenge.


Retention trends can provide valuable insight into the overall health of a workforce strategy.


## Workforce Decisions Are Based on Assumptions Rather Than Data


Many organizations track hiring activity and turnover metrics, but fewer have a comprehensive view of workforce health.


Organizations that regularly assess workforce health can identify challenges earlier and make more informed decisions about talent strategy.


## Workforce Readiness Starts With Visibility


Organizations cannot address workforce challenges they cannot see. The first step is understanding where workforce strengths and potential risks exist today.


[Take the Workforce Readiness Assessment](https://cbizsurvey.az1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_cVljL7Xbyr8dfMi) to receive your Workforce Health Score and gain insights into workforce demand, hiring efficiency, retention stability, and workforce capacity. Understanding these areas can help your organization identify opportunities to strengthen workforce readiness and support business goals.


#### Frequently Asked Questions


Misalignment can occur when business priorities evolve, but workforce planning, hiring efforts, retention strategies, or staffing capacity do not adapt at the same pace.


Workforce capacity helps determine whether an organization has enough people and resources to meet current and future business demands.


Employers should consider factors such as workforce demand, hiring efficiency, employee retention, workforce growth, and overall workforce capacity.
